claims.text: SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo resolved 12.47% (286/2,294) of the full SWE-bench test set and 18.00% (54/300) of SWE-bench Lite.
The previous best SWE-bench resolve rate before SWE-agent was 3.8%, achieved by a non-interactive, retrieval-augmented system.

SWE-agent's agent-computer interface (ACI) is an abstraction layer between the LM agent and the computer that defines the commands available to the LM and how environment feedback is formatted and returned.

SWE-agent's ablation on SWE-bench Lite showed it solves 10.7 percentage points more instances than a baseline agent using only the default Linux shell; the paper reports a 64% relative increase over Shell-only, both with GPT-4 Turbo.
SWE-agent's ACI design principles are: simple actions, compact and efficient actions, informative but concise environment feedback, and guardrails that mitigate error propagation and hasten recovery.

SWE-agent's search commands (find_file, search_file, search_dir) return at most 50 results per query; if a search exceeds that number, results are not shown and the agent is told to write a more specific query.
SWE-agent's file viewer shows a window of at most 100 lines, moved with scroll_down, scroll_up and goto, and displays the file path, total line count, lines omitted above and below, and line numbers.
SWE-agent's edit command takes a start line, end line and replacement text, replaces that line range in the open file, and the file viewer then automatically displays the updated content.
SWE-agent integrates a code linter into the edit command; invalid edits are discarded and the agent is asked to try the edit again, with a snippet of the file before and after the error shown.
SWE-agent collapses all observations older than the last 5 into a single line each, and omits all past error messages except the first, to keep context concise.
When a command produces no output, SWE-agent returns the explicit message "Your command ran successfully and did not produce any output" to make the result clear to the LM.
SWE-agent with Claude 3 Opus solved 10.5% of SWE-bench tasks, showing the ACI designed for GPT-4 Turbo is portable to a different LM.
Compared to the RAG baseline on SWE-bench Lite, SWE-agent is 8-13x more costly but yields a 6.7-fold improvement in % Resolved.
SWE-agent runs with a per-instance budget of $4; if a run exceeds it, existing edits are submitted automatically.
The SWE-agent authors found Llama 3 and DeepSeek Coder performed subpar in the agent setting, partly because context windows such as Llama 3's 8k were too small.
SWE-agent's execution environment and the SWE-bench evaluation framework both run in Docker sandboxed environments.

OpenHands' Docker Runtime uses a client-server architecture: the backend builds an 'OH runtime image' from a user-provided base image, launches a container, and runs an ActionExecutor inside it that initializes a bash shell, browser and plugins.

The OpenHands backend communicates with the action execution server in the sandbox over a REST API, sending actions and receiving observations, while the Agent and EventStream are spawned by the backend.

OpenHands tags runtime images with three hash-based tags (versioned, lock, source) so identical source and Dockerfile reproduce the same image and rebuilds can reuse existing layers; the lock tag hashes the base image name, pyproject.toml and poetry.lock.

OpenHands runtime plugins (e.g., Jupyter, VS Code, Agent Skills) are Python classes initialized when the action execution server starts, and OpenHands supports bind mounts, named volumes, and copy-on-write overlay mounts for sandbox volumes.

mini-swe-agent is about 100 lines of Python for the agent class, uses no tools other than bash (not even the LMs' tool-calling interface), and keeps a completely linear history where each step appends to the messages passed to the LM.
mini-swe-agent scores over 74% on SWE-bench Verified, and is evaluated on the SWE-bench (bash only) leaderboard that compares different LMs using the mini scaffold.

In an evaluation of 2,614 OpenHands trajectories from eight model backends on 60 SWE-bench Verified tasks, 10.7% of passing trajectories in a 1,815-trajectory subset were 'Lucky Passes' exhibiting regression cycles, blind retries, missing verification or disordered exploration.
Lucky Pass rates across the eight model backends ranged from 0.5% to 23.2%, and some models shifted by as many as five rank positions when ranked by process quality score instead of pass rate.
Amp's rebuilt CLI runs on a new architecture described as remote-controllable, compaction-first, plugin-powered, and faster, and threads started in the CLI can be remote controlled from ampcode.com.
